narrative:
The model estimates a 55% chance that you will leave your job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This means the system sees enough warning signs to lean toward expecting you will depart within the coming period.

Three main factors shaped this outlook, ranked by importance. First, your total years of professional experience stand out as the strongest influence, but in the direction of staying. Most employees the model expects to remain have similarly short overall experience of 1-5 years, so this actually worked in your favor and pulled the prediction downward.

The second most influential factor worked against you. Having received other job offers while at your current company strongly pushed the prediction toward leaving. This is relatively uncommon among people the model thinks will stay, where only about one in four report receiving such opportunities.

Third, your employment in the “other” sector also nudged the outcome toward departure. This sector makes up just 22% of the group predicted to stay, whereas medical and education roles dominate that stable group.

Taken together, the pull from external opportunities and sector outweighed the stabilizing effect of your experience level, tipping the balance just over 50%. 

The organization should discuss with you whether those external offers can be matched or if targeted support in recognition, training, and workload could strengthen your connection to the role. You may want to reflect on what would make staying feel more secure and satisfying.
